review.focus: Look for tactical motifs like unprotected pieces and pins on open files before making quiet moves, as seen on 10...Nd4 where 10...hxg5 won immediate material.

sections.text: Out of the Queen's Gambit Declined, you met White's aggressive h-pawn thrust with solid central play. You pushed queenside counterplay with 13...c4 and looked to break open lines, but 19...b5 allowed White to grab the initiative. After White's 21.Nxb5, you recaptured with 21...Qxb5, pinning the bishop on e2 along the rank and maintaining a strong attacking presence.

The game swung back in your favor after 24...fxe6 won a pawn and cracked White's center. However, the evaluation collapsed with 28...exf5, which walked straight into 29.Qxd5+; after 29...Kh8, White gained winning chances. White slipped with 30.Bxc4, pinning your queen to the rook on d5, but allowed 30...Qxe3+ to give you hope. Finally, 31...Nc5 dropped your defense, allowing 32.Rhe1 to win your queen.

review.headline: A sharp kingside storm breaks through after a critical defensive lapse

sections.text: Facing the London System, you opted for an early trade on g3 with 4...Bxg3 5.hxg3. While this removed White's bishop, opening the h-file gave your opponent a direct attacking avenue against your kingside once you castled into it.

White quickly centralized the queen and launched their kingside pawns with 11.Qh4 and 12.g4. Here, you tried 12...Nd5, unleashing a discovered attack from your queen on d8 against White's queen on h4, but it allowed White to continue pushing with 13.g5. The defensive resource was 12...Nh7, which also acts as a discovered attack on the h4-queen while actively blockading the h-file.

White gave you a window of relief with 14.Ne5, but 14...g6 proved fatal. Opening up your king's pawn shield while the h-file was already compromised allowed 15.Qxh6, leaving your king without defense against mate.

review.turning_point: The game was decided by 14...g6, which collapsed your kingside defense and allowed 15.Qxh6 with unstoppable mating threats.
review.focus: When your opponent attacks along an open file, prioritize piece blockades over pawn moves around your castled king, as seen on 12...Nd5 and 14...g6.

review.headline: A sharp Petrov opening unravels under tactical pressure

sections.text: You handled the Petrov's Defense well early on, quickly punishing White's loose 6.b3 with 6...Bb4+! to seize initiative. However, after exchanging dark-squared bishops, the game leveled out as both sides developed their pieces toward the center.

The game grew tense around move 12. White played 12.Bb5, creating a pin on your knight against your king on e8. Rather than capitalizing with dynamic active play, you responded with 12...a6, allowing White to trade pieces and unpin comfortably.

Trouble mounted as your bishop became a target on d5. After you played 16...Rfe8, reinforcing a pin on the e-file against e4, White struck with 17.c4. Giving up your bishop with 17...Bxc4 handed White a decisive material advantage, and 18...Qxd4 lost your queen after 19.Qxd4 before your clock ran out.

review.turning_point: The collapse began with 17...Bxc4, which surrendered a bishop instead of retreating to e6, leaving White completely winning.
review.focus: Track your minor pieces' safety against advancing enemy pawns before committing to squares like d5, avoiding decisions like 17...Bxc4.
